title: Insulation Resistance Test: 4 Foolproof Steps With PI
text:
Electrical Safety & Standards

 Insulation Resistance Test: 4 Foolproof Steps With PI and DAR

 A simple DC test that reveals moisture, dirt and ageing in motor, cable and transformer insulation before it fails.

 
 Megger Test 
 Polarization Index 
 DAR 
 Temperature Correction 
 




 An insulation resistance test applies a high DC voltage between conductors and earth and measures the tiny leakage current that flows. The result, in megohms, shows whether insulation is clean, dry and healthy.


 
 Hello everyone, today we are going to learn how an insulation resistance test works, how to choose the test voltage, and how to read PI, DAR and temperature corrected results with confidence.


 
 
 
 What Is an Insulation Resistance Test?


 An insulation resistance test measures how well the electrical insulation of a motor, cable or transformer resists DC current. The instrument, often called a megger, applies 500 to 5000 V DC and displays resistance in megohms or gigohms.


 Good insulation lets only a tiny current pass. Moisture, dirt, oil and cracks create leakage paths that lower the reading.


 
 
 Image credit: Motors@Work 
 

 The total current has three parts, capacitive charging current, absorption current and leakage current. The first two fade with time, while leakage stays, which is why timed readings are so useful.


 It is a key part of predictive and preventive maintenance for motors and cables. Trending readings over years often tells more than any single value.


 4 Foolproof Steps to Perform the Test


 
 1
 Isolate and Discharge
 Switch off, lock out, prove dead and discharge the equipment to earth.


 2
 Select Voltage and Connect
 Pick the test voltage and connect between conductor and earth.


 3
 Apply and Record
 Record readings at 30 seconds, 1 minute and 10 minutes.


 4
 Correct and Discharge
 Correct to a base temperature, then discharge the winding again.





 Step 1 is a safety step, never skip it. Follow lockout tagout and your electrical isolation permit before touching any conductor.


 Step 4 matters because long cables and large windings store charge like a capacitor. Discharge for at least as long as the test voltage was applied.


 Choosing the Test Voltage


 
 
 Equipment AC Rating Typical DC Test Voltage 

 Up to 100 V 100 to 250 V 

 440 to 550 V 500 to 1000 V 

 2400 V 1000 to 2500 V 

 4160 V and above 1000 to 5000 V or higher 

 



 These values come from the Megger insulation testing guide. Using too high a voltage on low voltage electronics can damage them, so disconnect drives and control cards first.


 For a quick minimum check, Megger gives the old one megohm rule. Insulation should be about 1 MΩ per 1000 V of operating voltage, with a minimum of 1 MΩ.


 PI, DAR and Temperature Correction Formula


 
 PI = R10 min ÷ R1 min 
 DAR = R60 s ÷ R30 s 
 R40 = Rt × 0.5^((40 minus t) ÷ 10) 

Rt = reading at winding temperature t in °C

Worked example at 30 °C:
R30 s = 600 MΩ, R1 min = 800 MΩ, R10 min = 2000 MΩ
DAR = 800 ÷ 600 = 1.33
PI = 2000 ÷ 800 = 2.5
R40 = 800 × 0.5^(10 ÷ 10) = 800 × 0.5
 Corrected 1 minute reading = 400 MΩ at 40 °C 



 Resistance halves for about every 10 °C rise in temperature, so readings must be corrected before comparing. Always record winding temperature and humidity with each result.


 PI is a ratio, so temperature affects it much less than single spot readings. That makes PI a more reliable health indicator for large motors.


 How to Judge the Results


 
 PI Above 4
 Excellent insulation condition.
 Best for: clean, dry windings
 Excellent 

 PI 2 to 4
 Good condition, normal for most machines.
 Best for: routine acceptance
 Good 

 PI 1 to 2
 Questionable, often wet or dirty windings.
 Best for: cleaning and drying
 Questionable 

 PI Below 1
 Poor insulation, do not energize.
 Best for: repair or rewind
 Poor 




 Megger lists a DAR of 1.4 to 1.6 as good and above 1.6 as excellent. Values between 1.0 and 1.25 are questionable.


 Motors@Work notes that PI above 5 can point to brittle epoxy, and PI loses meaning when the 1 minute reading exceeds about 5000 MΩ. Use judgement rather than a single number.


 Types of Insulation Resistance Test


 
 Spot Reading Single 60 second value

 Time Resistance PI and DAR over time

 Step Voltage Readings at rising voltages

 Trend Record Compare with past results

 Decision Run, clean, dry or repair




 The spot reading is quick but sensitive to temperature. The time resistance method, which gives PI and DAR, is almost independent of temperature.


 The step voltage test raises voltage in stages. A falling reading at higher voltage reveals cracks or contamination that low voltage tests miss.


 Where the Insulation Resistance Test Is Used


 
 Motors
 Before first start and after long shutdowns.


 Power Cables
 After laying and during periodic checks.


 Transformers
 Winding to winding and winding to earth checks.


 Switchgear
 Busbar and breaker insulation checks.


 Generators
 Stator and rotor winding assessment.


 Panels and Wiring
 Commissioning of new installations.





 For motors, the insulation class also sets the thermal limit. Our guide on motor insulation classes explains Class B, F and H ratings.


 Transformer IR checks are part of routine tests and site acceptance. Record results with the date and temperature for future trending.


 Weak insulation is not only a reliability problem but also a safety one. Leakage to a metal frame can create touch voltage, as explained in electrical shock causes and prevention , so good earthing and regular testing go together.
